text:
She saw again that accursed female with goat’s feet, half naked, who, with her right arm raised, seemed to command her to stop. She turned, and on the other side she saw Berto, who did not dare move to detain her, did not dare speak for fear of frightening her, and kept watching her, seeking to divine from her gestures the decision she would make.

She returned to her armchair, let herself fall into it, and did not say a word.

There followed, in this way, an anguished silence of several minutes, during which Loredana and Berto stared keenly at each other, motionless, as though scrutinizing one another; but Berto could endure it no longer, approached her again, and seized her hands.

“Stay!” he said, his voice veiled by passion. “Stay! I implore you! I know you do not love me, and that does not frighten me....”

He was trying to remove one of her gloves; she noticed and unbuttoned it with a quick gesture, offering him her bare hand and wrist to kiss; but when she felt those avid lips upon her flesh, she turned her head away, almost in disgust.

“No!” she said. “Wait!”

She seized the cup and drained it avidly, then held it out to Berto again so that he might pour her more, and again she drank; but, catching sight of herself in the mirror, she threw the empty cup to the floor, where it shattered.

“What do you want to do with me?” she then said.

“Everything you command me to do,” Berto replied. “I am free; I can leave today, tonight, tomorrow, whenever you ask me.”

“Yes,” Loredana declared. “We shall leave at once. We shall go to Rome.”

She broke into such a harsh, sardonic laugh that Berto looked at her in alarm.

“To Rome,” Loredana repeated. “I was supposed to go there with Flopi; I shall go with you. Is it not the same? Am I not your mistress? Did they not want me to be your mistress? One man or another, it matters little.... Why do we not go to Sirmione as well?... I want to trample upon all my past, I want to destroy every memory, I want nothing to remain, nothing at all of what was so dear to me, and what would make me blush!... Ah, you do not know the horror I feel for life!... You think of nothing but taking possession of me; I can see it in your eyes, and you do not understand that I am no longer alive, you do not understand that I hate you, and the nearer you come to me, the more I hate you!...”

Berto did not reply, but the hand that held the young woman’s hand loosened its grip; he drew back, struck by the savage vehemence of those words.

“Why do you want me?” Loredana continued, casting him a contemptuous glance. “I love Filippo, and I am sacrificing myself for him. Is that not clear? Is it not clear that I want to ruin myself in order to save him? Have I not told you already! And I chose you in particular so that he would despise me so much that he would no longer seek me out!... And you lend yourself to this game?... If I consented to become your mistress, that would be the moment when I loved Filippo most, because it would be the gravest sacrifice I could make for him.... And you did not understand that? How must I tell you that I shall never love you?”

Constrained by the ferocious logic, which seemed dictated by that need to bite and destroy with which Loredana felt her whole being quivering, Berto at first found no answer; then he uttered the one phrase that explained every madness:

“But I love you,” he said. “I love you, Loredana; and I know nothing else....”

The young woman looked at him, sensing that he was not lying; he seemed subdued and defeated to her, and she pitied him.

“Come now,” she murmured, rising, “let me go!”

“Where, where do you want to go?” Berto asked, taking a step toward her. “Where do you want to go, like this?”

She had started toward the door, without a hat, like a madwoman.

Berto looked at her, elegant and slender in her smooth amethyst-colored dress, gracefully adorned with a strip of dark fur that ran around her breast and along the very edge of the skirt like a little snake.

She was going out, leaving, fleeing; suddenly she had felt that the sacrifice was too repugnant, that it was better to die, to rest, to think of no one anymore, and she had remembered the deep black canal that flowed in front of Berto’s house.

The hour was late, the light dim, and few people were abroad on that winter evening. Loredana could have thrown herself into the water and drowned there without anyone coming to her aid.

“Where do you want to go?” Berto repeated.

They met on the threshold and stared at each other, his eyes blazing with desire, hers lost in despair; but because she meant to go on, he seized her by the arms and held her back.

Loredana broke into laughter again.

In her mouth she had the taste of that mud from which human beings drink their fill, that mud which is all of life, and an unquenched burning scorched her veins, as though she had swallowed liquid fire....

Someone behind Berto—perhaps the half-naked female with goat’s feet—suggested a thought to him: the young woman would never decide either to leave or to stay, either to live or to die; she had to be forced.

He abruptly drew her to his breast, sealed her mouth with his own, giving her so long a kiss that it seemed he wished to drink her life, her soul, her blood; he felt Loredana slowly yielding, falling backward, and followed the movement without taking his mouth from the longed-for mouth, and laid her upon the broad divan.




XVII.


It was a joyous spring, that of 1894 in Venice. A boundless host of foreigners descended from every part of the world, women and men already intoxicated with delights and desire, their souls vibrating with that sensual romanticism inspired by languid Venice.

New passions and new dramas sprang up amid that throng of people, and on certain evenings Saint Mark’s Square became a prodigious drawing room through which the fashionable women of New York and Paris, London and Vienna, Berlin and St. Petersburg wandered, leaving in their wake a trail of exotic perfumes.

They saw Venice through the eyes of legend and history, and their souls were transformed, pouring themselves out and becoming perverted amid the treasures of art and the deathly silence of the voluptuous city. The gondola, slow and caressing, agile and silent, made them dream the erotic dreams and swift tragedies of novels; the night, whether illuminated by moonlight upon the streams and canals, or dark, or veiled, seemed to them as enigmatic and extravagant as in no other city in the world.
